section.title: The Locust Plague
section.sectionRationale: The book opens with a catastrophe so severe it must be told to the next generation: wave upon wave of locusts has stripped the land bare. Joel reads this disaster not as random misfortune but as a summons, a herald of the Day of the LORD, and he calls elders, drunkards, priests, and farmers alike to wake, wail, and turn to God.
section.thesis: A devastating locust plague is a trumpet blast: it lays bare the fragility of life apart from God, and it points beyond itself to the nearness of the Day of the LORD, calling the whole community to fast, cry out, and return.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the charge to remember and tell; the fourfold locust and the ruined land; the call to mourn as priests and farmers grieve; and the cry to the LORD as even the beasts pant for Him.

verses.text: This is the word of the LORD that came to Joel son of Pethuel:
Hear this, O elders; and give ear, all who dwell in the land. Has anything like this ever happened in your days or in the days of your fathers?
Tell it to your children; let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation.

What the devouring locust has left, the {{arbeh|swarming locust}} has eaten; what the swarming locust has left, the young locust has eaten; and what the young locust has left, the destroying locust has eaten.
Wake up, you drunkards, and weep; wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it has been cut off from your mouth.
For a nation has invaded My land, powerful and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion, and its fangs are the fangs of a lioness.
It has laid waste My grapevine and splintered My fig tree. It has stripped off the bark and thrown it away; the branches have turned white.

units.label: A call to mourning
units.note: the offerings cut off, the land in grief

verses.text: Wail like a virgin dressed in sackcloth, grieving for the husband of her youth.
Grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD; the priests are in mourning, those who minister before the LORD.
The field is ruined; the land mourns. For the grain is destroyed, the new wine is dried up, and the oil fails.
Be dismayed, O farmers, wail, O vinedressers, over the wheat and barley, because the harvest of the field has perished.
The grapevine is dried up, and the fig tree is withered; the pomegranate, palm, and apple, all the trees of the orchard, are withered. Surely the joy of mankind has dried up.

units.label: A call to repentance
units.note: consecrate a fast, cry out to the LORD

verses.text: Put on sackcloth and lament, O priests; wail, O ministers of the altar. Come, spend the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God, because the grain and drink offerings are withheld from the house of your God.
{{qadash|Consecrate}} a fast; proclaim a solemn assembly! Gather the elders and all the residents of the land to the house of the LORD your God, and cry out to the LORD.
Alas for the day! For the {{yomYHWH|Day of the LORD}} is near, and it will come as destruction from the {{shaddai|Almighty}}.

units.label: Even the beasts pant for You
units.note: the cry from a scorched land

verses.text: Has not the food been cut off before our very eyes, joy and gladness from the house of our God?
The seeds lie shriveled beneath the clods; the storehouses are in ruins; the granaries are broken down, for the grain has withered away.
How the cattle groan! The herds wander in confusion because they have no pasture. Even the flocks of sheep are suffering.
To You, O LORD, I call, for fire has consumed the open pastures and flames have scorched all the trees of the field.
Even the beasts of the field pant for You, for the streams of water have dried up, and fire has consumed the open pastures.

arbeh.gloss: The most common Hebrew word for locust, from a root meaning to multiply or be many. It names the vast, teeming swarm that darkens the sky and devours everything green. Joel piles up four terms for the locust in one verse to picture wave after wave of destruction, leaving nothing for the next. The same insect was the eighth plague that fell on Egypt.

qadash.gloss: To set apart as holy, to consecrate or sanctify. To consecrate a fast is to declare a sacred time, marking it off from ordinary life and dedicating it wholly to seeking God. The word calls the whole community to a solemn, God-focused response rather than mere private sorrow.

yomYHWH.gloss: The Day of the LORD, the central theme of Joel. It is the appointed time when God draws near to judge sin and to save His people, a day of darkness for His enemies and deliverance for the repentant. The locust plague is a near preview of that greater and final Day, which is near and comes as destruction from the Almighty.

shaddai.gloss: Almighty, a title of God stressing His overwhelming power. Joel makes a deliberate wordplay: destruction (shod) comes from Shaddai, the Almighty. The One who is more than able to bless is also more than able to bring the ruin that His holiness requires when His people persist in sin.

basic.context: Joel opens with a national emergency: a plague of locusts has swept through the land in waves, eating the crops, the vines, and even the bark from the trees. The grain and wine that fed families and supplied the temple offerings are gone. Joel tells the people this is so unheard of it must be passed down for generations, and he reads it as a warning from God.
basic.hermeneutics: This really happened; the fields really were stripped. But Joel does not treat it as bad luck. He sees the disaster as a sign pointing beyond itself, a small and near preview of the great Day of the LORD. His aim is not to explain insect behaviour but to wake a comfortable people and call them to turn back to God.
basic.originalLanguages: Joel stacks four words for locust in verse four to picture relentless wave after wave. He calls the people to consecrate, qadash, a fast, to set apart a sacred time to seek God. And in verse fifteen he names his great theme, the Day of the LORD, yom YHWH, with a pun: destruction, shod, comes from the Almighty, Shaddai.
basic.typology: The locust army that no one can resist foreshadows the greater judgment of the Day of the LORD. The ruined offerings, grain and wine cut off from God's house, point ahead to the true bread and true vine, Jesus, who is never cut off from His people. The scorched land groaning for water anticipates the world's longing for the restoration only God can bring.
basic.christ: The plague strips away every false security and leaves people crying out to God, which is exactly where the gospel meets us. Jesus is the true grain and true vine that the locusts could never touch, the offering that is never cut off. He bore the destruction from the Almighty in our place so that the Day of the LORD becomes, for those who trust Him, a day of rescue.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over locusts; He can use the smallest creatures to humble a nation. He is holy and will not let sin go unaddressed, so He sends the plague as a wake-up call. Yet the very fact that He warns, and invites the people to cry out to Him, shows a God who disciplines in order to draw His people back, not to destroy them.
basic.crossReferences: The locusts recall the eighth plague on Egypt, Exodus 10. The Day of the LORD is developed by Amos, Zephaniah, and others among the Twelve. Jesus calls Himself the true vine, John 15, and the bread of life, John 6, the harvest the locust can never spoil.
basic.oneStory: Joel's plague is one scene in the long story of a God who lets ruin fall so that people will stop trusting in bread and wine and turn to Him. It points forward to the true harvest, Jesus, and to the final Day when God will judge all evil and satisfy His people forever.

context.literary:
Joel is a book of voices and commands. Almost every verse of the first chapter is an order, and the orders are addressed to a changing audience: the elders and everyone in the land in verse 2, the drunkards in verse 5, the farmers and vinedressers in verse 11, the priests and ministers of the altar in verse 13, and finally the whole assembly in verse 14. Each group is called to the same two actions, to listen and to grieve. Then the prophet does what he has told others to do, and in verses 19 and 20 he himself cries out to the LORD, with the beasts of the field joining him. The chapter is therefore not only a description of a disaster. It is a liturgy being assembled in front of the reader.

The opening in verses 2 and 3 uses a rhetorical question and a command to remember. Nothing like this has happened in living memory or in the memory of the fathers, and it is to be handed down to the third generation. That frame turns a bad season into a story the nation will tell. The central body of the poem alternates between the description of the damage and the people who feel it. Verses 4 to 7 describe the attacker, verses 8 to 10 the grief that follows, verses 11 and 12 the farmers' ruin, and verses 13 to 15 the summons to the temple. Verses 16 to 20 then return to the damage in a second round, this time heard as prayer.

A series of repeated words holds the chapter together. 'Dried up' and 'withered' sound across the orchard in verses 10, 12 and 17 and again for the streams in verse 20, so that the whole chapter is bracketed by drought. The idea of being 'cut off' is stated for the wine in verse 5, for the offerings in verse 9 and for the food and joy in verse 16, so that loss moves from the table to the altar to the heart. The chapter begins with a creature that eats and ends with a fire that eats, and in between the land groans.

There is no date by the reign of a king, which is unusual among the prophets. Joel is introduced only as the son of Pethuel, and the book simply begins with the word of the LORD. That choice puts the weight on the event and its message, rather than on the political calendar.
context.historical:
The Near East knew locusts, and ancient farmers feared them. Deuteronomy 28:38 to 42 lists locusts among the curses that would fall on a disobedient nation, and 1 Kings 8:37 includes locusts among the calamities for which a person might pray toward the temple. In Judges 6:5 the Midianites are compared to a swarm of locusts because of their number. The prophet Amos had already said that the LORD sent the locust against Israel's gardens, and 'yet you did not return to Me,' Amos 4:9. Joel's hearers would have known that a locust plague was both a natural event and a covenant sign.

The temple setting matters to this chapter. In verses 9, 13 and 16 the grain and drink offerings are no longer being brought, because there is no grain or wine to bring. Under the law the daily offering was accompanied by flour, oil and wine, Numbers 28:5 to 7, so a failed harvest meant a silent altar. The priests who 'minister before the LORD' are in mourning because the very rhythm of worship has been stopped by the plague. The consequences of a crop failure were therefore spiritual and not only economic.

The date of the book is uncertain. Joel names no king, and he addresses the elders and priests, which has led some to place him early, before the monarchy's reforms, and others after the return from exile when the temple community was led by elders and priests. In the Hebrew Bible Joel stands second among the Twelve, after Hosea and before Amos, and the Greek order differs. The wording of the book connects with other prophets, so that Joel 3:16 and Amos 1:2 share the line about the LORD roaring from Zion. Nothing in the first chapter depends on settling the date, because the point of the plague is the same wherever it fell.

The call to fast and to gather the community at the house of the LORD matches national practice elsewhere. King Jehoshaphat proclaimed a fast and gathered Judah to seek the LORD in the face of an invasion, 2 Chronicles 20:3 and 4, and the king of Nineveh called for sackcloth and crying out to God, Jonah 3:5 to 9. In a world where disaster was read as a divine message, the right response was to go to the sanctuary.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws on the story of Egypt in a way that readers of the Torah would catch. The eighth plague of Exodus 10 was a locust plague, and God told Moses that the purpose was 'that you may tell your children and grandchildren,' Exodus 10:2. Joel uses the same pattern of telling the children in verse 3 of this chapter, but this time the plague has fallen on God's own people. Egypt's story of judgment is told to the next generation in order to warn them, and now Israel is Egypt's seat.

The chapter then becomes one of the central statements of the Day of the LORD. Verse 15, 'Alas for the day! For the Day of the LORD is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty,' is almost the same sentence as Isaiah 13:6, and it is close to Ezekiel 30:2 and 3. Amos 5:18 to 20 had warned that people who longed for the day would find it darkness. Zephaniah 1:14 uses the same 'near' language. The theme runs through the Twelve, and Joel is where it takes its fullest shape.

The book's later chapters carry the chapter forward into the New Testament. Peter on the day of Pentecost quotes Joel 2:28 to 32 to explain the outpouring of the Spirit, Acts 2:16 to 21, and Paul quotes Joel 2:32, 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' in Romans 10:13. Revelation 9:3 to 11 pictures a plague of locusts from the abyss, with details that echo Joel, and Revelation 6:12 to 17 takes up the darkened sun and the question of who can stand on the great day.

The detail of the offerings stopped is also carried through. The picture of grain and drink offerings 'cut off' from the house of the LORD in verse 9 is answered in Joel 2:14, which hopes that the LORD may leave a blessing behind, 'grain and drink offerings for the LORD your God.' The chapter's loss is therefore the setting for the rest of the book's restoration.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Joel meant his hearers to read a farming disaster as a message addressed to them. The first chapter presses three points. The first is that the event is unprecedented and must be remembered, because a generation that forgets will be hit again. The second is that every group in the community has a stake in it, from the drunkard who loses his wine to the priest who loses his offering, and none can say it is someone else's problem. The third is that the right place to take a disaster is the house of the LORD, in fasting and prayer.

He also meant them to feel the gap between what they had assumed and what was true. The people had lived as if the harvest were a right. When it was gone, the joy went with it, verse 12, and Joel wants them to see how much of their happiness had been resting on a gift. The loss of the offerings made the point more sharply, because it showed that their worship was bound up with the same provision.

Above all, the chapter points beyond itself. The plague is the nearest thing to a trumpet that the people could hear, and verse 15 says what it is announcing: the Day of the LORD. Joel's aim is that the nation will not stop at grieving over the crops but will see what the crops are saying and turn to the God who sent the warning.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a specific plague and the community's loss, and it prescribes a specific response for that community: gather, fast, put on sackcloth and cry out. It is not a rule that every natural disaster is a direct punishment for the sins of those who suffer, and the rest of the Bible resists that conclusion. Jesus says that those killed when a tower fell were not worse sinners than others, Luke 13:4 and 5, and the book of Job warns against reading suffering as a verdict. Joel is applying the covenant to Israel, where God had told the nation that locusts could come as a warning, and it does not give a modern believer a way to diagnose a drought.

What carries forward is the pattern of response. A community in crisis takes it to God together, with honest grief and with public repentance, and does not simply endure it in private. The call to elders, priests, farmers and drunkards shows that no one is exempt. The priests are told to lead in lament, which gives church leaders a model for what to do when the community is in pain.

The language of sackcloth and fasting is an outward form for an inward posture. Joel 2:13 will say that hearts and not garments must be torn, and the New Testament does not tell believers to wear sackcloth. What it keeps is the call to humble ourselves before God in the face of trouble, James 4:9 and 10.

debates.question: Are the locusts literal insects or a picture of an invading army?

views.label: A real locust plague
views.case: The chapter speaks of crops, orchards and pastures stripped, and the description of the attack in verses 4, 7 and 10 to 12 fits the destruction locusts cause. The four names in verse 4 and the comparison to teeth of a lion in verse 6 are comparisons used for locusts elsewhere. Exodus 10 shows locusts were a known instrument of the LORD. Most readers hold this view for chapter 1, and see the army language of chapter 2 as an intensification.

views.label: A human army pictured as locusts
views.case: Verse 6 calls the invader 'a nation' with teeth like a lion and says it has come against 'My land.' Some read the whole book as a poem about a human invasion, with locusts as the metaphor, noting that Judges 6:5 compares Midian to locusts and that the book mentions foreign nations in chapter 3.

views.label: A literal plague that becomes a picture of the end
views.case: Others see a real plague which the prophet uses as a window onto the final judgment, so that the literal event and the future Day of the LORD are layered. Revelation 9 reuses the locust imagery in an apocalyptic way.

debates.bearing: The footnote at verse 4 admits that the precise identification of the four kinds of locust is uncertain. The weight of the chapter falls on the effect and on the response, not on the entomology. The detail of ruined vines, cut off offerings and panting beasts makes a literal plague the most natural reading of chapter 1, while the way Joel treats it as a sign makes the other views understandable.

debates.question: When was Joel written?

views.label: Early, in the ninth century BC
views.case: Joel names no king and has the elders and priests as the community's leaders. This may fit a time when a young king was under priestly guidance, as in 2 Kings 11 and 12. The book's position among the earlier prophets in the Hebrew order may reflect this.

views.label: After the exile, in the fifth century or later
views.case: Joel speaks of the scattering of Israel among the nations and of the sale of the people of Judah to the Greeks in chapter 3, and has the temple community with priests, elders and offerings in the foreground. These features fit the period after the return from exile.

views.label: Undated on purpose
views.case: Some say the lack of a date is itself a clue, as the book is shaped to apply to every generation that experiences judgment and hope, with the Day of the LORD always near.

debates.bearing: The date does not change what the chapter asks of the reader. In each case the plague is a call to repentance with the Day of the LORD in view. The matter is important for historical background but not for the book's central message.

study.originalLanguages:
The book begins with two verbs for communicating a memory. 'Hear' in verse 2 is shama, and 'tell' in verse 3 is saphar, which also means to recount or count. The verb of telling and the phrase about children and grandchildren come from Exodus 10:2, where the eighth plague was to be told to later generations. Joel uses the vocabulary of Egypt for a disaster in Judah, which means the people are being asked to see themselves in the story they thought belonged to someone else.

The four locust names in verse 4 are gazam, arbeh, yeleq and chasil, rendered 'devouring, swarming, young and destroying.' The BSB footnote says the precise identification is uncertain, and the four may be stages of growth or kinds of locust, or simply a poet's repeated words. In 2:25 the same four appear in a different order, with the swarming locust first and the devouring locust last, so the list is not a fixed formula. What matters is the effect: the word 'left' in each line shows that each wave takes what the one before it missed.

Verse 6 calls the invader a goy, a nation, the ordinary word for a foreign people. It is also 'powerful and without number,' much as the book of Judges compares an innumerable host to a swarm of locusts, Judges 6:5. By using the word for a nation of a swarm of insects Joel blurs the line between insect and army, which is part of the effect of the poem. The language of 'My land' is the language of a landlord, and it tells us that the owner of the land is the LORD and that the invader has come with His permission.

In verse 8 the word for 'husband' is ba'al, the Hebrew word that also names the Canaanite storm god. The phrase 'the husband of her youth' is one of the everyday uses of the word for owner or master. Hosea 2:16 has God say that His people will call Him 'my Husband' and no longer 'my Master,' and uses a different word for the first title to avoid the name of the god. Joel's use is the plain one: a young woman mourns for the one she married.

In verse 14 the phrase 'solemn assembly' is atsarah, the word for a restraint or a holding back, used for the closing assembly of the festivals in Leviticus 23:36. The verb 'cry out' is the verb for a shout for help. With 'fast,' tsom, they make up the three parts of a national emergency gathering. Isaiah 1:13 shows that the people could hold such an assembly and still be rejected when it was merely routine, so Joel's stress on the heart in the next chapter belongs here.

In verse 15 the interjection 'Alas for the day' has an exact echo in Ezekiel 30:2, where the same cry is raised over Egypt. The word 'near' is qarov, which appears again and again in the Day of the LORD passages. It describes a day that is not far off, not one that is already here.

The verb 'cut off' in verses 5, 9 and 16 is karat, the verb used in the idiom 'to cut a covenant.' It is not argued that Joel is making a pun, but a hearer who knew the idiom would feel the weight of a covenant's gifts being cut off.

Finally, 'pant' in verse 20 is the verb that Psalm 42:1 uses of a deer longing for streams of water. The animals do what the psalmist does, and the humans in this chapter have not yet. The verb 'consumed' for fire in verses 19 and 20 is the ordinary verb to eat, the same verb that describes the locusts' work in verse 4, so that the whole chapter is a story of things being eaten.

typology.type: Locusts on God's own people, Joel 1:4 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The eighth plague on Egypt, Exodus 10, was a judgment on those who held God's people. Here the same instrument falls on the people themselves, and the thing that had been told as a warning to the nations is now a warning to Israel. The pattern points forward to the final locusts of Revelation 9:3 to 11, where creatures like horses prepared for battle come out of the abyss against those who do not have God's seal. The correspondence is one of divine method: God has used swarms to judge. The type falls short because Joel's plague is temporary and corrective, with a way back, while Revelation's is a final sealing of judgment on the unrepentant.

typology.type: The offerings cut off, Joel 1:9 and 13
typology.fulfillment: The grain and drink offerings, the daily gifts that kept fellowship with God, are stopped. The loss shows how fragile the old system was, since it depended on harvests and on a priesthood that could be silenced. In Christ the offering is never cut off. Hebrews 10:11 to 14 says that priests stand daily offering the same sacrifices, but this Priest offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down. At the table Jesus takes bread and the cup, Luke 22:19 and 20, as the new meal of fellowship. The type falls short because the offerings were gifts that depended on the land, while Christ's offering is of Himself and does not depend on the seasons.

typology.type: The bride mourning her husband, Joel 1:8
typology.fulfillment: The people are told to wail like a young woman grieving for the husband of her youth. The image is of a relationship broken by loss. In the New Testament Jesus uses the bridegroom picture of Himself, saying that when the bridegroom is taken away the guests will fast, Matthew 9:15, and Paul speaks of presenting the church to Christ as a pure virgin, 2 Corinthians 11:2. The correspondence is that the people's grief for what they have lost is the grief of a bride, and the true Bridegroom comes. The type falls short in that Joel's mourning is for a loss that the people brought on, whereas the church's separation from her Bridegroom is temporary, and is ended at the wedding supper, Revelation 19:7.

typology.type: The parched land and panting beasts, Joel 1:19 and 20
typology.fulfillment: The streams are dried and even the animals look up to the LORD. The picture of creation crying out for water is a standing image of a world waiting for the water that only God gives. Jesus stands in the temple on the last day of the feast and cries out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37, and on the cross says 'I am thirsty,' John 19:28. The correspondence is that the thirst of creation is taken up in the thirst of Christ and answered in the Spirit. The type falls short because the beasts can only pant, whereas Christ gives living water to those who come.

study.christ:
The first way this chapter leads to Christ is through the question it forces on the reader: where should a person take a disaster? Joel's answer is the house of the LORD, in confession and cry. The New Testament gives the same answer but gives the house a Person. Jesus is the one in whom God's people now draw near, Hebrews 4:16, and the great High Priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, Hebrews 4:15. In Joel the priests are told to put on sackcloth and lead the lament. In Christ the Priest does not just lead the lament but bears what the lament is about.

It leads to Christ through the stopped offerings. The central grief of verse 9 is that the grain and drink offerings are cut off, so that the way of approach has failed. This is a kind of picture of what sin does to every human attempt at worship. In Christ the approach is given back on different terms. Hebrews 10:14 says that by one offering He has perfected for all time those who are being made holy. The offering that cannot be cut off is the one that was made once by a priest who lives forever, Hebrews 7:24 and 25.

It leads to Christ through the Day of the LORD. Verse 15 announces destruction from the Almighty, and the question that the first hearers must have asked is the one that chapter 2 will put in words, who can endure it? The New Testament answer is that the Day of the LORD is the day of Jesus Christ. Paul tells the Corinthians that Christ will keep them blameless on 'the day of our Lord Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 1:8, and Peter says the Day will come like a thief, 2 Peter 3:10. Where Joel saw the dread of the Day, the apostles see the same Day with a person standing in it for those who are in Him. Romans 5:9 says that we will be saved from the wrath through Him.

It leads to Christ through the way Joel's book ends up being quoted. On the day of Pentecost, Peter says that the pouring out of the Spirit is what was spoken by the prophet Joel, Acts 2:16, and that 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' Acts 2:21. The scorched land of chapter 1 is the starting place for the book's movement toward the Spirit poured out on all flesh, and the one who pours Him out is the risen Christ, Acts 2:33. The thirst of the beasts in verse 20, and of the people, is answered in a Person.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The locusts are not a code for the devil or a veiled picture of the cross, and it would be wrong to find Christ in each detail of the damage. The right way to read it is by the text's own movement: loss, lament, the nearness of the Day, and the later promise of the Spirit and of deliverance on Zion. Those themes are what the New Testament takes up and applies to Jesus. The chapter provides the problem, a people stripped and a Day approaching, and Christ is the answer the rest of Scripture gives.
study.god:
The chapter shows the LORD as the owner of the land. The invader has stripped 'My land,' and the vine and fig tree are 'My grapevine' and 'My fig tree' in verse 7. The people had been treating the land as theirs. Joel shows that they were tenants, and that the Owner can send creatures to take back what He lent. That ownership is not a threat but a truth about reality: every harvest was a gift in the first place.

It shows Him as sovereign over small creatures. The locust is described as His agent, in the same way that in Exodus 10 He brought the swarm on an east wind, and in 2:25 He will call it 'My great army that I sent against you.' This is a sobering truth, and it is also a comfort, because it means the disaster is not random. The God who sent it is the God who can end it, and who can be asked.

It shows Him as a God who warns. The first chapter is a trumpet before the blow. The Day of the LORD is called near rather than present, and the people are given time and a way of response. That is consistent with the character of God that the later chapter quotes from Exodus 34:6, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger. The very fact that the prophet is sent is a sign that the LORD wants a response rather than a ruin.

It shows Him as holy. The loss of the offerings and the grief of the priests make clear that fellowship with God is not a right that survives sin. He is the Almighty, Shaddai, the One before whom destruction itself is under command, verse 15. The same holiness that makes the Day of the LORD terrible is what makes His presence the one thing worth seeking.

It shows Him as the God who hears the cry of creation. In verses 19 and 20 the prophet calls and the beasts of the field pant for Him. The Psalms say that God gives food to the beasts and to the young ravens when they cry, Psalm 147:9, and Jesus says that the Father feeds the birds of the air, Matthew 6:26. The chapter closes with an appeal to the LORD as the one who is able to provide.

For worship, the chapter teaches that lament is a form of faith. The people are not told to hide the losses but to name them aloud at the house of God. It teaches that the right thing to do when blessings are taken away is to go to the Giver. And it teaches that our worship should be the sort that can survive an empty barn, since God Himself and not the gifts is the object of it, a lesson that Habakkuk 3:17 and 18 will express when the fig tree does not blossom and the prophet still rejoices in the LORD.

crossReferences.note: The eighth plague on Egypt, brought by an east wind, covered the land until it was dark and consumed all the plants and fruit. Joel's description borrows the scale and the totality, and the comparison shows that what God did to Pharaoh He can do to His own people when they turn from Him.

God tells Moses to let the plague be recounted to children and grandchildren. Joel 1:3 uses the same pattern, so that the prophet is saying the story of this plague must be told as the Exodus plagues are told, as a lesson about who the LORD is.

Among the curses for covenant disobedience are sowing much seed and harvesting little because locusts consume it, and vineyards whose grapes the worm eats. The locust is therefore a covenant sign, and Joel's hearers would have seen their situation in the list.

The LORD says that the locust devoured the fig and olive trees, 'yet you did not return to Me.' Amos shows the purpose of such plagues, which is to bring the people back, and Joel's call to cry out is the proper response that Amos says was refused.

'Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty.' The sentence is almost identical to Joel 1:15. The prophets share a common vocabulary for the Day, and Isaiah applies it to the nations while Joel applies it to Judah.

Ezekiel calls on the people to wail, 'Alas for that day,' for the Day of the LORD is near, a day of clouds. The same cry as Joel 1:15 is used against Egypt, showing that the Day is not limited to Israel but touches every nation.

The locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation. This explains the discipline of the invader in Joel, and prepares for chapter 2, where the advance of the army is described as orderly, with no swerving from the course.

The deer pants for streams of water and so the soul longs after God. In Joel 1:20 the beasts of the field pant for the LORD when the streams dry up. The same verb is used, showing that thirst for water and thirst for God belong together.

God's own answer to the lament of chapter 1. 'Yet even now,' He says, return with all your heart, for He is gracious and compassionate, and He may leave a blessing, 'grain and drink offerings for the LORD your God.' The cut off offerings of 1:9 are the very thing He may restore.

Peter explains Pentecost with words from Joel, the Spirit poured out and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord saved. The book that begins with a scorched land is shown to end, in Christ, with the Spirit on all flesh.

The locusts of the abyss look like horses prepared for battle, with teeth like those of lions. The details draw on Joel's description of the invader, and show that Joel's locust imagery was read as a pattern of the final judgment.

Though the fig tree does not blossom and there is no fruit on the vines, the prophet will rejoice in the LORD. This is the worship that survives what Joel 1:12 describes, and it shows what faith looks like when the harvest fails.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 had said that the ground would be cursed because of human sin, with thorns and toil. Joel 1 is a picture of what that curse looks like at its fiercest, and the answer to the question of why creation can turn on its inhabitants. The land that was given as a gift to Israel, flowing with milk and honey, is shown as something the LORD can withdraw. The Eden pattern lies close beneath the surface: a garden of plenty, then a wasteland. Chapter 2 will say it outright, with the land before the army like the Garden of Eden and behind it a desert.

What the chapter answers from earlier is the covenant structure of blessings and curses in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The locust was named there, and the arrival of the plague is a sign that the covenant is being applied. The exodus plagues are also behind it. Egypt learned who the LORD is through a plague of locusts, and Israel is now being taught the same lesson as the nations were.

What it sets up is the whole message of the Day of the LORD, which runs through the prophets and into the New Testament. Joel makes the day a near thing by means of a present event. His call to cry out and return is taken up in the next chapter, which turns from the army to the offer of grace, and then to the promise of the Spirit and the restoration of the years the locust has eaten. The prophets after him, Amos, Obadiah, Zephaniah and Malachi, develop the Day further.

The story comes to rest in Christ, who stands in the Day. The Day of the LORD that Joel feared becomes the Day of the Lord Jesus, and the question of whether a person can stand on it is answered by whether he is in Christ. At the cross the land itself went dark, and the offering that cannot be cut off was made. The Spirit that Joel promised was poured out in the city where the offerings had been stopped.

The new creation is the place where there is no more curse, and where the river of the water of life runs through the city and the tree of life bears fruit every month, Revelation 22:1 to 3. The thirst of the beasts and the loss of joy are finally answered. The God who took the harvest has promised to restore the years, and the new creation is that restoration in full.

quiz.q: How does Joel want the people to understand the locust plague?

options.text: As a divine summons and a near preview of the Day of the LORD, calling them to return to God.
options.note: Joel reads the disaster as a sign pointing beyond itself to God's judgment and call.

options.text: As a serious agricultural loss they must simply endure and rebuild from.
options.note: The loss is real, but Joel's point is spiritual, not merely economic.

options.text: As bad luck with no meaning behind it.
options.note: Joel insists the plague carries a message from God, not mere chance.

options.text: As proof that God has abandoned His people forever.
options.note: The plague is a call to return, and the book moves on to promised restoration.

quiz.q: Why does Joel stack four different words for locust in verse 4?

options.text: To picture wave after wave of total devastation, leaving nothing behind.
options.note: The piled-up terms convey relentless, complete destruction.

options.text: To identify four separate species with scientific precision.
options.note: The exact species are uncertain; the point is the totality of the ruin, not taxonomy.

options.text: To show the plague came in stages over several seasons of loss.
options.note: Successive waves are implied, but the main thrust is the completeness of the destruction.

options.text: To suggest the damage was actually quite minor.
options.note: The repetition stresses overwhelming, not minor, loss.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the grain and drink offerings being cut off (verse 9)?

options.text: Worship itself has collapsed, since the offerings depended on the ruined harvest.
options.note: The disaster reaches into the house of the LORD, halting the daily offerings.

options.text: The priests have simply lost part of their personal income.
options.note: There is real loss to the priests, but the deeper issue is the breakdown of worship.

options.text: The people have chosen to stop worshiping God.
options.note: The offerings stop because the harvest failed, not by a deliberate refusal to worship.

options.text: It shows the offerings never mattered to God anyway.
options.note: The offerings mattered; their loss is precisely why the priests mourn.

quiz.q: What response does Joel call the whole community to make?

options.text: To consecrate a fast, gather in solemn assembly, and cry out to the LORD.
options.note: Joel summons everyone to set apart a sacred time and turn to God together.

options.text: To grieve privately until the crops eventually recover.
options.note: Sorrow is right, but Joel calls for a public, God-directed turning, not just private grief.

options.text: To organize better defenses against the next plague.
options.note: The call is spiritual repentance, not disaster planning.

options.text: To ignore the loss and carry on drinking as before.
options.note: Joel wakes the drunkards to weep; complacency is exactly what he confronts.

quiz.q: What is the wordplay in verse 15, 'destruction from the Almighty'?

options.text: Shod, destruction, sounds out of Shaddai, the Almighty, tying the ruin to God's own power.
options.note: The Hebrew pun links devastation directly to the character and hand of God.

options.text: It simply names two unrelated ideas that happen to appear together.
options.note: The pairing is a deliberate sound-play, not a coincidence.

options.text: It hints that the destruction is powerful, without any link to God's name.
options.note: The power is real, but the point is that the ruin flows from Shaddai Himself.

options.text: It means God is unable to prevent the coming ruin.
options.note: The Almighty is the source of the judgment, not powerless before it.

questions: Joel calls a comfortable people to wake up and see God's hand in their loss. Where might God be using a disruption in your life to get your attention?
The plague stripped away wine, food, and joy until only a cry to God remained. What securities are you leaning on that could be stripped away, and what would it look like to lean on God instead?
Joel summoned the whole community, from drunkards to priests, to fast and pray together. How does corporate repentance differ from private regret, and where might your church need it?
The offerings were cut off, yet in Christ the true offering is never cut off. How does knowing Jesus as the bread and vine that never fail steady you when earthly provision feels fragile?
Even the beasts pant for God in the drought. When life dries up, do you instinctively cry out to the LORD, or do you turn to something else first? What would change that?

translationNotes.note: The four Hebrew terms for locust are difficult to distinguish precisely; BSB renders them devouring, swarming, young, and destroying. The uncertainty of the exact species does not affect the meaning: successive waves of total devastation.
The phrase 'destruction from the Almighty' renders a Hebrew wordplay, shod (destruction) echoing Shaddai (Almighty); Shaddai is a title of God stressing His overwhelming power.
